stories.headline: Update: Jeffries Nominated for Speaker as Trump Signals Openness to Compromise With Incoming Democratic Congress
stories.summary:
House Democrats this week nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for the Speakership, setting up what would be his historic election as the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber. Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) was also elected to a leadership post as the first woman in her role. Democrats took the House and the Senate in the midterms, and several House races remain uncalled. The 119th Congress left town Saturday after a week of confirmations and bills, with Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and other leaders voicing frustration over low attendance.

President Trump said Saturday in a Fox News interview with Kayleigh McEnany that the Democratic-controlled Congress presents an opportunity to compromise on immigration and health care. He offered rare praise for Jeffries even after Jeffries called top aide Stephen Miller a "stone-cold racist"; Trump defended Miller as a "good person." Jeffries told The New York Times he is open to working with Republicans but has not yet spoken extensively with GOP leaders.

The administration is also bracing for oversight. Late Friday Trump signed an executive order directing federal contractors to notify the White House of congressional requests for their communications and to withhold material the administration deems privileged. Republicans and administration allies describe it as protecting executive confidentiality, while Democrats and critics say it is an attempt to stymie oversight before they take control in January. Democrats are also expected to scrutinize ICE tactics, after masked agents detained two people on a Seattle-Tacoma airport jet bridge Saturday, prompting condemnation from Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson.

Republicans, meanwhile, are debating the causes of the midterm losses. Some, such as former Sen. Sam Brownback, say voters rejected Trump personally rather than his policies, citing inflation and gas prices, while others are already positioning for the 2028 nomination.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Calls Putin a 'Killer' After Trump Calls Him a Friend; Russian Strikes Continue
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN that Vladimir Putin is a "killer" and an enemy, responding to Donald Trump calling the Russian leader his "friend" before Thursday's trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelensky said it was up to Trump how to describe Putin, but that such language suggests Putin "doesn't feel enough pressure." Trump, speaking Friday, doubled down on the description, said Putin would "love to end the war," and said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

Russian attacks continued overnight. Officials said two people were killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih, with more injuries in Kharkiv and Rivne. On Friday at least nine people were killed in strikes on Kyiv bridges and western railway stations, in what Zelensky called the biggest attack this year: 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

Zelensky told the BBC that Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge were a "fair response" to 109 Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges, rejecting Putin's claim that the span is purely civilian. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting visited Kyiv to show European unity and called a Russian cruise missile that hit Poland during coalition exercises an "outrageous provocation." Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said the missiles' guidance systems make it very unlikely they strayed off course because of Ukrainian electronic warfare. Poland has called the incident a provocation, and no injuries were reported.

stories.headline: Update: COP31 Climate Talks Go Into Overtime With Fossil Fuels Absent From Draft Deal
stories.summary:
The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, extended into an unscheduled extra day on Saturday as negotiators sought a final agreement, even as work crews boxed up the venue. Hopes are slim that the added talks will yield concrete plans to cut fossil fuel use. The draft final text has drawn strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels.

A letter sent Saturday by 100 civil society groups to the co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, warned they were on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UN has held, with only hours left to save it. Observers at the venue described a bleak atmosphere with dwindling food and water and no sign of progress. Teresa Anderson of ActionAid International said no one knows what is happening behind closed doors.

The backdrop is stark. The UN said before the talks that the world will likely overshoot the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and Climate Action Tracker found progress has stalled for five years. Experts say drastic cuts to coal, oil and gas emissions are needed to avert the worst effects, while vulnerable nations, including small island states, are pressing for stronger action. The outcome of the extended session is the main development to watch.

stories.headline: South Korea's Education Minister Resigns Over College Exam Cheating Scandal
stories.summary:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned Sunday over the cheating scandal and chaotic countermeasures surrounding Thursday's national college entrance exam, the Suneung. President Lee Jae Myung, who has called for an overhaul of the exam system, accepted the resignation. Choi said he could not escape criticism that the government failed to prepare in advance.

The crisis began a week earlier when Han Won-seok, the top scorer on April's national tax accountancy exam, admitted using a micro-camera, a phone and AI tools to cheat. In response, authorities rushed in new measures just days before the Suneung, which about 500,000 students took. For the first time, the national disaster alert system was used to catch cheaters, with three alerts sounding on phones nationwide between 08:00 and 15:00, even on silent mode and on tourists' roaming phones.

Candidates also had to cover buttons on clothing and submit to eyewear inspections, which left even honest test takers anxious. The education ministry said 111 candidates were found with unauthorized smart devices. The exam heavily shapes career paths for millions of South Koreans, and the episode has intensified debate over academic dishonesty in the age of AI.
